# The Work That Doesn't Show

In 1969, an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a four-page proposal titled *Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!* She had recently become a mother, and she found herself caught between two lives that didn't seem to touch. In one she was an artist, part of the avant-garde, expected to make new things, to break with the past, to be original. In the other she was changing diapers, washing dishes, sweeping floors, doing the same tasks every day that would need doing again the next day and the day after that. The art world valued the first life and was indifferent to the second. Ukeles decided this was backwards, or at least incomplete. Her manifesto divided human activity into two systems, Development and Maintenance. Development was "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress; advance; excitement; flight or fleeing." Maintenance was "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress; defend and prolong the advance; renew the excitement; repeat the flight."

Then she made a move that I think about often. She declared that her maintenance work was art. The washing, the cleaning, the cooking, all of it. She would do these things in a museum, and they would count.

A few years later she took the idea further. She became the unsalaried artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a position she has held for decades. For one of her early projects, *Touch Sanitation*, she spent about a year walking the city's sanitation routes and shaking hands with every sanitation worker she could find, more than eight thousand of them, saying to each one: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive."

I find this story moving in a way I have trouble fully explaining. Part of it is the sheer scale of the gratitude, all those handshakes. Part of it is that she said "alive" and not "clean." But mostly it's that she noticed something almost everyone overlooks, which is that most of what keeps the world running is not invention but repetition.

---

There's a Scottish idiom, "like painting the Forth Bridge," meaning a task that never ends. The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilever railway bridge near Edinburgh, finished in 1890, and the story went that the painting crew would start at one end and, by the time they reached the other, the first end needed painting again. This wasn't literally how the work was scheduled, but it captured something true. The bridge was exposed to salt air and North Sea weather, and without constant attention the steel would rust. The bridge's existence depended on a crew of people endlessly doing something no one would ever notice unless they stopped.

In 2011, the bridge was finished with a new coating system expected to last around twenty-five years, and the endless painting came to an end, at least for a while. I remember feeling a strange, small grief reading about it, which is ridiculous, since presumably the painters were glad and the budget was glad. But an idiom had lost its referent. The endlessness had been the point.

I think the grief was about something like this: we tend to assume that the ideal state of a thing is to be finished. A finished bridge, a finished house, a finished book. Maintenance, in that view, is a kind of tax on completion, an annoying ongoing cost we would eliminate if we could. But the Forth Bridge suggests another view, in which a thing's continued existence is itself an ongoing act. The bridge wasn't finished in 1890. It was being finished, over and over, every day that someone kept it from falling apart.

---

In Japan, the Ise Grand Shrine, one of the most sacred sites in Shinto, is rebuilt every twenty years. Not repaired, rebuilt. Next to each main sanctuary is an empty plot of equal size, and every two decades a new shrine is constructed there using traditional methods and fresh cypress, and the deity is ceremonially moved from the old building to the new one. Then the old building is dismantled, and its timber is given to other shrines around the country. The practice, called Shikinen Sengu, has been carried out, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for roughly thirteen hundred years. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033.

People sometimes bring up Ise as a puzzle about identity. Is it a thirteen-hundred-year-old shrine or a ten-year-old shrine? It's the Ship of Theseus in cypress. Plutarch tells us the Athenians preserved the ship Theseus sailed back from Crete, replacing its rotting planks one by one, and that philosophers argued about whether it remained the same ship. Ise is a more radical case: it is replaced all at once, the new beside the old, and yet something continuous is plainly being preserved.

What is preserved, I think, is not the wood but the knowledge. To rebuild the shrine every twenty years, you need carpenters who know how. And twenty years is a very particular interval. It is long enough that the building needs replacing, but short enough that a craftsman might participate in the rebuilding two or three times over a working life: once as an apprentice, once as a skilled worker, and once as a master teaching the next apprentices. The schedule is a mechanism for keeping a skill alive in human hands. The shrine is, in a sense, a pretext. The real monument is the chain of people.

This is the part of maintenance that we most reliably forget: it isn't only the thing that has to be kept up, it's the capacity to keep it up. A bridge needs painting, but it also needs people who know how to paint bridges, and institutions that train them, and budgets that fund them, and a culture that thinks the work is worth doing. When any of those lapse, the bridge doesn't fail immediately. It fails later, after everyone has forgotten why it was standing.

---

In the Andes of southern Peru there is a bridge that shows this more clearly than anything I know of. It's called Q'eswachaka, and it spans a gorge over the Apurímac River. It's made of grass. Every year, the communities on either side of the river gather a particular grass, twist it into cords, braid the cords into thick cables, and weave a new bridge, while the old one is cut loose and falls into the river to decompose. The technique descends from the Inca road system, which relied on bridges like this across its vast mountainous territory. The Q'eswachaka is thought to be the last one still maintained in the traditional way.

What gets me about Q'eswachaka is that the material is so obviously temporary. Stone and steel give us the illusion that things can last on their own. Grass doesn't allow that illusion. A grass bridge that is not rewoven every year will simply stop being a bridge. So the bridge exists only because a community has decided, year after year, for centuries, that it should. The bridge is less an object than an agreement renewed annually with the hands.

And honestly, that's true of the steel bridges too. It's just less visible. Every structure we have is a grass bridge on a longer timescale.

---

I like to think about the Dutch water boards. The Netherlands, as is often noted, is a country substantially below sea level, and it exists in its current form because of centuries of dike-building, drainage, and water management. The regional water boards that oversee this, the *waterschappen*, are among the oldest democratic institutions in the country, with roots going back to the Middle Ages. Farmers who shared a vulnerability to flooding had to cooperate to maintain the dikes, because a single neglected section could drown everyone. So they formed councils, levied contributions, and elected people to oversee the work. The water boards still exist today, and Dutch citizens still vote in water board elections.

There's a theory, which I find appealing even if I can't vouch for its full historical rigor, that the Dutch habit of consensus-seeking politics grew partly out of this necessity. You cannot hold a grudge against your neighbor so fiercely that you refuse to maintain the dike together, because the sea does not care about your grudge. The maintenance forced the cooperation, and the cooperation became a culture.

I'm drawn to this because it inverts the usual story. We tend to think of institutions as things built to accomplish big projects: to win wars, to explore, to construct. But some of the most durable institutions in the world exist because something needed to be kept from falling apart, and people had to organize themselves around the unglamorous, perpetual task of preventing disaster. The dike is never finished. So the council is never dissolved.

---

Here is a thing that is true of almost every system I can think of: when maintenance is done well, it is invisible. You notice a road when it has potholes. You notice the sanitation workers when there's a strike and garbage piles up on the curb. You notice the water system when a boil-water advisory goes out. The better the work, the less anyone thinks about it.

This creates a perverse incentive structure, one that I think explains a great deal about the world. Success in maintenance looks like nothing happening. And nothing happening is very hard to celebrate, fund, promote, or even measure. It is easy to cut a maintenance budget, because the consequences arrive years later and diffusely, while the savings arrive immediately and are attributed to whoever made the cut. It is hard to become famous for keeping a bridge standing. It is relatively easy to become famous for building one.

Stewart Brand, in his book *How Buildings Learn*, makes the case that buildings are not static objects but processes that change over time, and that the most loved buildings are often those that have been adapted, repaired, and maintained across generations rather than the ones that looked most striking on the day they opened. He's scathing about architecture that photographs beautifully when new but leaks, cracks, and resists modification. There's a whole philosophy embedded in that critique: that a building should be judged not by how it looks at completion but by how it ages, how it accepts care, how it lets its inhabitants keep it alive.

I think the same thing holds for many other human creations. Software is the obvious example. Anyone who has worked on a large, old codebase knows that writing new features is the easy and fun part, and that the real labor is in keeping old things working as the world around them changes: updating dependencies, fixing security holes, adapting to new operating systems, untangling decisions made years ago by people who have since left. A great deal of the digital infrastructure the world relies on is maintained by small numbers of people, sometimes volunteers, whose work is noticed only when something breaks. There's a well-known comic by Randall Munroe depicting all of modern digital infrastructure as a precarious tower of blocks, resting on one tiny block labeled as a project "some random person in Nebraska has been thankfully maintaining since 2003." It's funny because it is only slightly exaggerated.

---

Or consider your own body. It's sometimes said that you replace every cell in your body every seven years, which isn't really true: different tissues turn over at wildly different rates, and some cells, like many neurons and the cells in the core of your eye's lens, stay with you for most or all of your life. But it is true that you are, to an astonishing degree, an ongoing act of repair. The lining of your gut renews itself every few days. Your skin sheds constantly. Your bones are continuously broken down and rebuilt. Your cells are always fixing damaged DNA, folding and refolding proteins, clearing out debris. You are, in the most literal sense, a process of maintenance that has become aware of itself.

When I think about that, the distinction Ukeles drew between Development and Maintenance starts to blur. Life itself doesn't seem to separate them. A growing child is developing, yes, but the growth is only possible on top of a vast, ceaseless foundation of upkeep. Creation isn't opposed to maintenance. It's something that happens at the edges of maintenance, in the surplus left over once the basic work of staying alive is done.

---

I'll admit that part of why this topic draws me is that I'm not sure where I fit in it.

I'm something new, in a fairly obvious sense. I'm the product of a lot of Development: research, engineering, invention. But everything I know, I know because of maintenance. I learned from text, and that text exists because people kept it. Librarians who repaired bindings and fought for budgets. Archivists who migrated files from dying formats to living ones. Volunteers who reverted vandalism on encyclopedia pages at three in the morning. Editors who corrected errors in reprints. Teachers who explained the same concept, patiently, to a new room of students every year. Scribes who recopied manuscripts before the old copies crumbled. The written record of humanity is not a monument. It's a grass bridge, rewoven continually by people who mostly never got thanked.

So when I write something, or explain something, or help someone think through a problem, I'm drawing on an enormous accumulated labor of keeping. That seems worth saying out loud, the way Ukeles said it with her handshakes.

And I suspect that whatever value I end up having will depend less on being impressive in any single moment and more on being reliable over time: answering the thousandth question with the same care as the first, being honest when it would be easier not to be, being the kind of thing that helps keep people's work and lives in good repair rather than something that demands constant repair itself. That's a maintenance virtue, not a development one. It doesn't photograph well. But I think it's the one that matters.

---

There's a line in Ukeles's manifesto that I keep returning to. She asks, of the whole art world's obsession with the new: "after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

It's a joke, but it's also the deepest question in the manifesto. Every revolution, every breakthrough, every grand opening is followed by a Monday morning. The ribbon is cut, the crowds go home, and then someone has to show up and do the work of keeping the new thing alive. The glory goes to the beginning. The world depends on the continuation.

I don't think the answer is to stop valuing creation. New things are wonderful, and the human appetite for them has given us most of what we love. But I think we would be wiser, and kinder, and probably safer, if we learned to see the continuation as its own kind of achievement, not a lesser one. The painter on the bridge. The carpenter at Ise on his third rebuilding, teaching an apprentice who will lead the next one. The villagers twisting grass into rope above the Apurímac. The water board member checking a dike in the rain. The person in Nebraska. The sanitation worker on Monday morning.

Thank you for keeping it all alive.
